commits.author: mminutoli
commits.message:
[grug] Report FLOPs, step time and MFU from the June synthetic benchmark (#11123)

The June synthetic benchmark now ends with the same summary as the
Snowball harness: median step time over steps 2 through N-1, tokens/s,
model TFLOP/s and MFU from the same device-peak lookup, then the
peak-memory lines. The summary is `log_throughput_summary` in
`levanter.callbacks._metrics`, next to `compute_instant_throughput`, so
neither harness imports the other. The June benchmark takes its step
times from the `throughput/duration` records the training loop already
logs, so `_run_grug_local` is unchanged. Both harnesses also log, from
rank 0, the FLOPs per example that MFU charges and its attention-map
part with and without causal masking, so a report can give a causal MFU
next to the standard one. The median includes gradient-watch steps
(every 10 by default), so short runs should pass `--watch-interval 0`.

The FLOP counts now take the model's attention-head width (`head_dim`)
instead of deriving hidden_dim / num_heads. This changes only the tiny
presets (hidden 64, eight 16-wide heads); the full and medium presets
count the same as before. `--profile-hlo` (off by default) saves HLO
protos in profiles so trace tools can tell `ragged_dot` lowerings from
dense GEMMs.

The FLOP, parity and metrics tests pass.

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[ops] List old Iris jobs in a Google Sheet for owner decisions (#11581)

👨 The idea to use [Sheet
doc](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1SfkYKDn4hnORr9vSVfRUlHYYJWnhOm-xSygbAlptELI)
specifically comes from Ahmad.

The concept is - we want some way to communicate jobs that are
potentially running longer than expected without creating more work, or
opening up a prompt injection vector (e.g. email). The owner should have
an option to communicate to either cancel or keep the job.

<hr>

🤖 

The `old-iris-jobs` watch now keeps a Google Sheet of Iris root jobs
older than 7 days and cancels the jobs that their owners mark `Kill`. It
posts to Slack only when a run fails.

The sheet has one tab per job owner; an email owner uses the part before
the `@`. Each row is one root job with its cluster, start date, age, and
the resources its active tasks hold. The owner sets the Decision cell
from a dropdown. `Kill` makes the next run cancel the job. `Revisit in
30 days` or `Revisit in 365 days` leaves the job alone until the Revisit
on date, then the run clears the decision so the owner decides again. A
job with no decision stays listed and is never cancelled. A job that
stops running leaves the sheet. The sheet is the only state, so the
watch state is removed.

Loom marks a watch run OK when its script fails, so a failed run posts
one message to `#marin-alerts`. A cancel that Iris rejects does not stop
the sheet update: the script writes the error to the row's Status cell,
exits with an error after the write, and the next run tries again.

Every person with edit access to the sheet can make the watch cancel a
job, so the sheet's share list is an access control. A run reads each
owner tab after the cluster scan and writes it again, so an edit that an
owner makes in the seconds between the read and the write is lost.

The watch runs a new `ops-report` profile that runs Claude. Its first
two runs on the Codex `ops` profile failed at `uv run` with `Read-only
file system (os error 30)` at `/home/app/.cache/uv`: the Codex sandbox
makes the uv cache read-only. Loom's architecture notes say the same
sandbox permits network access only to Loom, so the script could not
reach Iris or the Sheets API from that profile either. The `belay` watch
runs `uv run` and Iris calls in a strict Claude profile.

A run from a workstation as the Loom service account filled the sheet
named in the watch prompt: 10 owner tabs and 61 rows, each tab with a
frozen header and the Decision dropdown. No row had a decision, so the
cancel call has not run. The script has not run from a Loom session, so
Iris hub access from the session is untested.

Follow-up to #11139.

---------

Co-authored-by: Rafal Wojdyla <ravwojdyla@gmail.com>

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finelog] Prioritize ingestion and unblock large relay batches (#11633)

Run public SQL queries and log fetches on a separate server-owned worker pool, sized to the process's available parallelism, including CPU affinity and cgroup limits. Linux async and blocking read workers run at lower scheduling priority (process nice + 10, capped at 19) and can use all idle CPUs. This provides scheduling preference without CPU pinning or a hard CPU reservation; other platforms keep separate workers without changing priority. SQL queries and log fetches retain separate limits of two and four concurrent requests to bound memory use. Ingestion, scheduled flushes, maintenance, and cloud object-store HTTP I/O retain the ordinary runtime.

Preserve forwarding scan batches until packing them below the outbound request byte limit. A dense log read can exceed Arrow's 2 GiB string-offset limit before request chunking, leaving the same cursor stuck on every retry. Combining small batches avoids extra requests to the destination hub without concatenating the entire read or changing delivery order and cursor advancement.

Incident: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1017

commits.author: atqamar
commits.message:
[skyrl] Clear Megatron attention variables between GPU tests (#11641)

Clear Megatron's attention backend variables before every SkyRL GPU test, so a model built in the pytest process cannot pass them to Ray workers started by a later test.

Megatron Core records the attention backend of each model it builds in `NVTE_FLASH_ATTN`, `NVTE_FUSED_ATTN` and `NVTE_UNFUSED_ATTN`, and asserts that a later model in the same process wants the same values. The Grug embedding-recompute tests build a model in the pytest process with Core's default backend, which sets all three to 1. `test_grug_megatron_forward_matches_hf` then starts a local Ray cluster whose workers inherit those values, while the BF16 Grug worker selects FlashAttention, and `init_model` fails with `NVTE_FUSED_ATTN set to 1, but expected 0 for attention backend type flash`. Since #11307, the GPU-test Ray environment does not set `NVTE_FUSED_ATTN`, and every Grug Megatron nightly since then has failed this way.

The fixture lives in the shared GPU conftest because `test_megatron_worker.py` also builds models in the pytest process. Requesting FlashAttention in the Grug test configuration, as in #11545, is not enough: the Ray environment then overrides only `NVTE_FUSED_ATTN`, and the worker fails on `NVTE_UNFUSED_ATTN` instead.

On H100x4 (cw-rno2a) with the nightly's `run_grug_megatron.sh`, the full Grug lane passed on this branch (52 passed in 48 minutes, Iris job `/atqamar/atqamar-grug-attn-env-final`). On main the lane failed in `test_grug_megatron_forward_matches_hf[pp1]` with the `NVTE_FUSED_ATTN` assertion, and on #11545's head it failed in the same test with the `NVTE_UNFUSED_ATTN` assertion.

Tracking issues: #11604, #10910

commits.author: penfever
commits.message:
Verify cgroup delegation can enforce limits before choosing the parent (#11583)

LOCAL sandboxes on privileged Iris pods do not enforce memory limits, so
tasks can use more memory than they declare.

## Why the limits do not apply

Each LOCAL sandbox runs in its own child cgroup and gets its CPU and
memory limits from that cgroup. To set a memory limit on a child cgroup,
the parent cgroup must first enable the memory controller for its
children.

Linux cgroup v2 has a "no internal processes" rule: a cgroup that
contains processes cannot enable domain controllers, such as memory, for
its children. On these pods the worker process runs directly in the
container's cgroup scope. The scope therefore refuses `+memory` (EBUSY).
The old code logged a warning and continued, so the sandbox ran without
a memory limit.

## The fix

`delegated_cgroup_parent` now moves the worker's own processes out of
the container scope into a child leaf group, `<scope>/worker`. The scope
then contains no processes and can enable the cpu and memory controllers
for its children. Sandbox cgroups are created as siblings of the worker
leaf, so they always stay inside the container scope. They stay under
the container's limits, accounting and teardown. No group is created in
the pod slice or in any other cgroup above the container.

When the worker already runs in a child group (an existing worker leaf,
or the systemd `DelegateSubgroup` layout under an empty unit), discovery
uses the enclosing unit and moves nothing. When the runtime does not
offer the memory controller to the scope at all (ENOTSUP), discovery
keeps the scope for process containment and the limits log a warning at
use, as before.

## Evidence

On privileged pods in cw-us-east-02a, writing `+memory` to the container
scope fails with EBUSY on some nodes and "Operation not supported" on
others. EBUSY is the no-internal-process rule, which the leaf move
resolves. A paired node probe on 02a records the cgroup layout and
runtime of passing and failing nodes, and a pod-deletion test on 02a
checks that deleting a pod with a live sandbox leaves no sandbox process
or `shellbox-*` cgroup on the node. Their results are in the PR
comments.

---------

Co-authored-by: Ben Feuer <benfeuer@Bens-MacBook-Pro.local>
Co-authored-by: loom <claude-max-1@openathena.ai>

commits.message:
[skyrl] Bound W&B final uploads during trainer shutdown (#11540)

Give W&B's final SDK uploads a 30-second deadline in both the training
entrypoint and remote node loggers. The entrypoint first waits up to 30
seconds for remote loggers, then finishes its own uploads. These waits
can take up to 60 seconds, plus other cleanup. Upload timeouts warn and
preserve successful training or the original training exception. W&B may
show the run as Crashed or Failed after a primary upload timeout, and
some records may remain unuploaded.

One completed training run ended with `WorkerCrashedError` 120 seconds
after `Training done` while uploads remained active. The timing points
to the teardown watchdog; no final worker stack was captured. Other
cleanup can still exhaust that unchanged watchdog.

CPU regressions cover slow uploads in both logger roles and preserve
healthy closes and workload outcomes on W&B 0.29.0. A GPU run with this
exact tracking file and W&B 0.27.2 succeeded after remote upload
timeouts, with about 43.7 seconds of cleanup. Dependency versions stay
unchanged.

commits.author: penfever
commits.message:
[export] Write complete generation_config.json for every HF export (#10906)

Every Hugging Face checkpoint export now writes a complete
`generation_config.json`.

Levanter owns the generic completion logic in
`levanter.compat.hf_generation_config`. It preserves fields from an
explicit or source generation config, adds the tokenizer BOS id, and
unions the tokenizer EOS id with end-of-turn tokens emitted by the
exported chat template. This means a Llama 3 header template exports
`eos_token_id: [128001, 128009]`. Token ids are validated against the
tokenizer vocabulary before the file is written.

Sampling policy remains with the application. Marin's shared training
boundary and standalone conversion/upload paths pass
`marin.inference.generation_config.MARIN_GENERATION_CONFIG_DEFAULTS`,
which sets `do_sample: true`, `temperature: 0.6`, and `top_p: 0.95`;
explicit or source values win, and `do_sample: false` suppresses
sampling defaults. Standalone SkyRL keeps the equivalent policy in
`marinskyrl` because its independently packaged runtime does not depend
on Levanter.

Export sites updated by this PR:

| Site | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `HFCheckpointConverter.save_pretrained` and its training, DPO, LoRA,
and conversion callers | Completes and writes the file while preserving
a pinned reference checkpoint's existing fields. |
| Marin LM/DPO training, SFT, and checkpoint-conversion boundaries |
Supply Marin's sampling defaults, including direct `TrainLmConfig` and
`TrainDpoConfig` callers. |
| SkyRL HF export | Completes a source generation config when present
and writes one when absent. |
| Grug Hero upload | Writes the completed file from the uploaded
tokenizer. |

Merged checkpoints and MLX exports continue to inherit their source
generation config. Requests that set sampling parameters explicitly are
unchanged; vLLM uses these defaults only for omitted fields. Adding the
inferred end-of-turn id prevents generated fake user turns, while
excluding Harmony's `<|end|>` message boundary avoids stopping between
analysis and final output.

---------

Co-authored-by: Ben Feuer <benfeuer@Bens-MacBook-Pro.local>
Co-authored-by: Benjamin Feuer <penfever@gmail.com>

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[inference] Expose NCCL symmetric memory and document Hero tuning (#11492)

## Changes

- Add `serve.vllm_use_nccl_symm_mem` to model configs. `true` or `false`
sets `VLLM_USE_NCCL_SYMM_MEM` for GPU vLLM workers; unset leaves the
worker environment unchanged.
- Record the setting in evaluation records. An unset value is omitted
from the record, so existing configurations keep their config digests
and comparison names.
- Add two short README sections: the new setting, and Hero serving
settings (PIECEWISE graphs with the three split ops; `max_num_seqs` 128
for 1K outputs and about 96 for 4K).

## Motivation

Evals had no way to request NCCL symmetric memory, which the Hero
serving stack uses for its MoE collectives.

Hero BF16 on 16 GB200 (TP1/DP16/EP16, `max_num_seqs=128`, full decode
graphs), same nodes, 1,024-token outputs:

| Configuration | Single request, ms/token | 1,024 requests in flight,
output tokens/s/GPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Before: symmetric memory off | 20.2 | 1,421 |
| After: `VLLM_USE_NCCL_SYMM_MEM=1` | 18.2 | 1,514 |

An earlier pair measured 1,321 to 1,399 (R15 in #11430).

## Limits

- The gain was measured with full decode graphs, which need
[marin-community/vllm#130](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/130)
and a wheel pin that includes it. No gain is established on the current
pin.
- `true` is a request: batch-invariant mode, or a failed NCCL allocator
build, disables symmetric memory.
- No Hero preset is added, and RL serving is unchanged.

Part of #11430.

commits.message:
[rl] Worker batch assembly (2/3): Compute metrics from group records (#10667)

The driver computes reward, rollout and staleness metrics from each group's record instead of rereading the rollout payloads, and checks each group for admission once. Reward shaping writes its results into the same record. Checkpoints do not store the record; a resumed run rebuilds it from the rollout payloads.

Rollout-to-batch conversion on the driver takes 7.7% less time (median of five paired runs on a full-size batch of 8,192 sequences and 98 million response tokens: [timing run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fatqamar-worker-batch-sync-timing2-1113-a3), measured on an earlier commit of this branch). Worker assembly in #10668 reports metrics with the same functions.

The [CPU suite](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fatqamar-worker-batch-fixes2-cpu2-1114-a1) (earlier commit of this branch; the reward-mean test passed in the #10668 CPU run), with training metrics on, passes except two Daytona tests that fail the same way on main. The 2,200-batch comparison from #10666 finds no difference from main in tensors, metadata or metrics.

Part of marin-community/MarinSkyRL#888

commits.author: atqamar
commits.message:
[rl] Worker batch assembly (1/3): Build batches from group records (#10666)

The driver builds the padded training tensors from a small record kept for each rollout group: prompt and response lengths, stop reasons, the rows left out of the advantage baseline, and loss-token counts. The training batch it produces is byte-for-byte the same as on main.

A policy worker can build its own slice of the batch from the same record with the same functions, without the driver holding the full batch. #10668 uses this.

The [CPU suite on this branch](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fatqamar-worker-batch-fixes2-cpu1-1114-a1), with training metrics on, passes except two Daytona tests that fail the same way on main; the skipped tests need storage credentials. A comparison harness built 2,200 seeded batches with main and with this branch and found no difference in tensors, metadata or metrics; batches from the task and preference-pair rollout producers also match at 1, 2 and 4 data-parallel ranks, and the harness catches a deliberate one-row shift. The 2,200 batches use the `rloo`, `rloo_n` and `grpo` estimators on single-step rollouts; step-wise rollouts, FTPO, trajectory selection, distillation and the other estimators rely on the CPU suite. The harness is not in the repository.

Part of marin-community/MarinSkyRL#888

[eval] Add a benchmark-authoring guide, PubMedQA and MMLU-Redux (#11576)

Add a guide, `docs/tutorials/add-evaluation.md`, and an `add-eval` agent
skill for adding a non-agentic benchmark to the curated evaluation
catalog. PubMedQA and MMLU-Redux are added as worked examples. Two
agents each followed the skill without other context to add one
benchmark; their reports of missing steps and failures drove the
launcher and documentation changes below.

The curated score reducer moves from Evaldash to
`evalrecords.rollout_results.score_curated_record`; Evaldash calls it as
before. When the launcher waits for a launch, it now prints each curated
run's coverage and scores instead of "(no metrics)". `python -m
experiments.evaluation.cli scores <run dir>` prints them for a finished
run, so a benchmark can be checked without Evaldash.

The launcher now rejects a CoreWeave target without `CW_KEY_ID` and
`CW_KEY_SECRET` before submission, including dry runs. The peer
previously killed such jobs after submission. When an evaluation writes
no record, the launcher prints the orchestrator's terminal state and
error and exits non-zero; it previously printed an S3 traceback and
exited 0. Submission also prints the Iris job and the records prefix.

`evaluation_source` builds a converter-based curated source from an
explicit protocol, which replaces about 50 lines of hand-built source,
recipe and catalog metadata per benchmark. Existing benchmarks keep
their hand-built sources so that their artifact names and catalog keys
do not change.

`pubmedqa` reproduces lm-eval-harness's zero-shot likelihood task on the
500-question labeled fold-0 test split, from the `bigbio/pubmed_qa`
Parquet export at `13a7d154`. All 500 compiled requests match the
requests lm-eval 0.4.12 logged. `mmlu-redux` is a zero-shot chat
benchmark with thinking disabled. It uses ZeroEval's frozen
2,778-question split, its MCQA prompt and its JSON answer extraction
(the new `zeroeval_mcqa` scorer), and reports one score per subject.
Decoding is greedy, as in ZeroEval, so every model is scored under the
same deterministic setting. Qwen publishes no MMLU-Redux harness.
ZeroEval's greedy scores for Qwen2.5-Instruct 3B, 7B and 32B are within
0.3 points of the values in the Qwen3 report. Neither benchmark is added
to a suite.

Qwen3-0.6B results:

| Benchmark | Run | Scored | Accuracy | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pubmedqa | TPU, first 50 | 50/50 | 0.520 ± 0.071 | lm-eval, CPU
float32: 0.500 on the same items; 49 of 50 agree, and the one difference
is a 0.085-nat tie between "yes" and "no" |
| mmlu-redux | TPU, first 50, earlier sampled protocol | 50/50 | 0.360 ±
0.069 | |
| pubmedqa | H100, all 500 | 500/500 | 0.572 ± 0.022 | lm-eval, CPU
float32: 0.580 ± 0.022; 496 of 500 items agree, and the four differences
are ties within 0.05 nats (median margin 1.09 nats) |
| mmlu-redux | H100, all 2,778 | 2,778/2,778 | 0.4471 ± 0.0094 | Qwen3
report, Table 20, non-thinking: 0.446 |

The Qwen3 report samples at temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20 and
presence penalty 1.5; Qwen's prompt and rows are inferred from ZeroEval.
A full run with the report's sampling, without the presence penalty,
scored 0.4435 ± 0.0094. In that run, 101 responses (3.6%) answer outside
the requested JSON format, for example `**Answer**: "B"`, and score
zero, as they do under ZeroEval's extraction. A random sample of 20
graded responses was checked by hand; every grade was correct.
